source.title: On Large Batch Training and Sharp Minima: A Fokker–Planck Perspective

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper’s own experiments and analysis refine the claim that large batches converge to sharp minima: sharpness changes with batch size during training, but the asymptotic preference for flatter minima is independent of batch size. It does not measure the training–test generalization gap.
record.gate_note: The paper reports batch-size and momentum comparisons of Hessian Frobenius norm as a proxy for sharpness. It explicitly says the correlation between sharp minima and worse generalization is not studied here. No results measure test error or the training–test gap; cited generalization results are prior work and are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study measures Hessian sharpness trajectories and analyzes idealized SGD dynamics, but reports no held-out performance or training–test gap. It explicitly excludes studying sharpness’s correlation with generalization. Thus it tests neither V5’s large-batch generalization penalty nor V7’s magnitude-aware sharpness–gap relationship, nor any other listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors’ conclusion. More precisely, under their SDE assumptions, they claim an asymptotic preference for flatter minima, with a batch-size-independent relative preference between equal-loss minima, while convergence depends on batch size. They present experiments as corroboration. They explicitly caution that transferring asymptotic SDE results to SGD requires a uniform-in-time approximation that remains open for nonconvex losses.
record.recipe_differences: Studies batch-size and momentum effects on Hessian sharpness trajectories through an SDE/Fokker–Planck analysis and experiments; it does not measure the training–test generalization gap or use the original versions’ measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size changes convergence speed and finite-time sharpness; at a fixed learning rate, larger batch training reaches sharper minima in the reported comparisons. Momentum’s effect on final sharpness differs by architecture: ξ = 0.99 yields flatter minima for MLP and N1, but sharper minima for N2.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed learning rate, larger batches reach sharper minima in the reported experiments; sharpness trajectories also depend on the learning-rate-to-batch-size ratio.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch size and learning rate affect Hessian curvature trajectories during SGD training.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing momentum to 0.99 produces flatter minima for MLP and N1 but sharper minima for N2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effect of momentum on final Hessian sharpness depends on architecture.

record.peer_reviewed: Journal of Statistical Theory and Practice (stated in supplied metadata)
record.problems: Experiments use the Frobenius norm of the Hessian as a substitute for the determinant-based sharpness in the theory. Numerical plots are averaged over 100 repetitions but no uncertainty bars are stated in the supplied text. The paper explicitly says generalization correlation is not studied; its asymptotic conclusions concern the idealized SDE, and uniform-in-time approximation of SGD by SDE for non-convex losses remains open.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result measuring training error, test error, or the generalization gap was present. Numerical sharpness experiments are extracted in rows R1–R6; Figure 3 and Figure 4 curve values not stated in text are not reconstructed.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy under natural versus random labels.
Test error as width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected held-out performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer held-out performance under different tuning regimes.
Large-batch held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and whether recipe adaptations remove its penalty. Fixed epochs and varied batches alone do not test this outcome.
Dropout’s effect on held-out error across data sizes and regularization regimes.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with training–test gaps, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Test accuracy after removing highly memorized versus random training examples.

record.verdict_notes: Change the record’s tests/T5 classification and V5 tested_not_extracted status: curvature dynamics do not test the stated generalization versions. The experimental Frobenius norm is also distinct from the theory’s Hessian determinant and V7’s magnitude-aware sharpness.

versions.untested_parts: Memorization of random labels and test accuracy on natural or random labels.
Width beyond interpolation and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer held-out performance.
The paper varies batch size and reports sharpness dynamics, but does not compare held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets, so it does not test the version’s generalization penalty.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the training–test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.
